name: Ezeiza International Airport - Ministro Pistarini
before:
Argentina's main international gateway, at Ezeiza 22 km south south west of Buenos Aires, handling 85 per cent of the country's international air traffic. The inner-city Aeroparque Jorge Newbery takes domestic and regional routes, so a client connecting between the two faces a cross-city transfer.

Plan the ground journey. There are buses to central Buenos Aires and to Retiro bus station, and local services, but there are no trains at all.

The terminals were reorganised recently. A new Departures Terminal opened on 14 April 2023, 50,000 square metres over four floors and built for 30 million passengers a year. At that point the old Terminal A became International Arrivals and the old Terminal C became Domestic Arrivals, so older terminal guidance is misleading.

The airport covers 3,475 hectares and has been operated by Aeropuertos Argentina 2000 since 1998. It is a major hub for Aerolíneas Argentinas.
after:
Argentina's main international airport, at Ezeiza, south west of Buenos Aires. It is about 50 minutes from the city centre, according to the city's tourism board. The inner-city Aeroparque Jorge Newbery takes domestic and regional routes, so a client connecting between the two faces a cross-city transfer.

Plan the ground journey. The tourism board lists Tienda León shuttles to Puerto Madero in the city centre, city buses, taxis and remises (private hire cars).

Terminal arrangements keep changing. A new Departures Terminal opened on 14 April 2023: 50,000 square metres on four levels, built for 30 million passengers a year. Domestic and international arrivals have shared Terminal A since July 2026, and Terminal C now handles only domestic departures, Aeropuertos Argentina says, so older terminal guidance is misleading.

The airport covers 3,475 hectares and has been run by Aeropuertos Argentina since 1998. Aerolíneas Argentinas flies long-haul routes from here.

claims.claim: Argentina's main international gateway
claims.note: Four independent publishers agree it is the country's main international airport: the city's tourism board (most international flights arrive here), Aviacionline (16 August 2026: 'the main international airport of the country'; 28 January 2026: it led international traffic in 2025), the operator ('the most important in the country') and Wikipedia. The old '85 per cent' share is cut below: it is out of date. In review, 'gateway' became 'airport' (house style), as at Hangzhou and Kunming.

claims.claim: handles 85 per cent of the country's international air traffic
claims.wasBefore: handling 85 per cent of the country's international air traffic
claims.why: Out of date. Aviacionline's 2025 ranking (28 January 2026, from ANAC figures) gives Ezeiza 8,533,000 international passengers and Aeroparque 5,229,000 (up 39 per cent), the Buenos Aires airports together 87 per cent; ANAC counts 15,911,424 international passengers for the whole country in 2025, so Ezeiza's own share was about 54 per cent. Only Aviacionline gives Ezeiza's figure (ANAC's statistics portal timed out, the city statistics page Wikipedia cites answered 503, and ORSNA's site is known to answer 503), so no share is given. 'Main international gateway' stays.

claims.claim: runway works: from 25 October to 11 November 2026 only a shortened runway 11/29 (1,850 m)
claims.why: Held back: a warning that replaces nothing in the old text, and the most useful thing found for agents booking late October and early November 2026. Runway 17/35 has been under rehabilitation since 1 August 2026; from 25 October to 11 November 2026, while the crossing of the two runways is rebuilt, Ezeiza will use only runway 11/29, cut from 3,300 to 1,850 metres. Delta suspends its Atlanta and New York flights from 24 October to 10 November and United its Houston flights over the same period, American Airlines keeps a daily Boeing 787 from Miami and stops some 777 flights in Montevideo, and other airlines have rescheduled or added stops. One organisation only (Aviacionline, 16 April and 16 August 2026): no second publisher was found (AeroRoutes, which Aviacionline cites, had nothing on its front page). For Andy to decide.
